lessons.title: Feed Per Stage: Nursery to Finisher
lessons.body:
Pigs eat different amounts and types of feed as they grow. Knowing how much to feed at each stage saves money and keeps your pigs healthy. A pig's life is divided into stages: nursery (weaning to 10 weeks), grower (10 to 16 weeks), and finisher (16 weeks to market). Each stage has specific feed needs.

In the nursery stage, piglets are small and their stomachs are sensitive. They need highly digestible feed, often called creep feed or nursery pellets. A piglet will eat about 0.5 kg per day. Over 4 weeks, that's 14 kg per pig. For 20 piglets, you need 280 kg of nursery feed. This feed is expensive, so buy only what you need.

During the grower stage, pigs grow fast and eat more. They need grower feed with about 16% protein. Each pig eats around 1.5 kg per day. Over 6 weeks (42 days), that's 63 kg per pig. For 20 pigs, that's 1,260 kg. You can mix your own grower feed using maize, soya, and minerals to cut costs.

In the finisher stage, pigs are almost market weight. They eat about 2.5 kg per day. Over 8 weeks (56 days), that's 140 kg per pig. For 20 pigs, that's 2,800 kg. Finisher feed has less protein (14%) and more energy. You can use cheaper ingredients like cassava or maize bran.

Total feed for one pig from nursery to market: 14 + 63 + 140 = 217 kg. For 20 pigs, that's 4,340 kg. At 20,000 Naira per 50 kg bag, that's 1,736,000 Naira. Knowing these numbers helps you plan your budget and avoid running out of feed. Always buy feed in bulk to get discounts. Store feed in a dry place to prevent mold.

lessons.title: Calculating Feed Conversion Ratio
lessons.body:
Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) is a simple number that tells you how well your pigs turn feed into meat. It is the total feed eaten divided by the total weight gained. A low FCR means your pigs are efficient; a high FCR means they are wasting feed. Calculating FCR helps you spot problems early and make more profit.

To calculate FCR, you need two numbers: total feed consumed and total weight gained. For example, if you have 10 pigs and they eat 1,000 kg of feed over a period, and their total weight increases by 400 kg, then FCR = 1,000 Ã· 400 = 2.5. This means it takes 2.5 kg of feed to produce 1 kg of pig. 

You must weigh your pigs regularly. Use a livestock scale or a weigh tape. Weigh them at the start of the period and at the end. Also, keep track of how much feed you give them. Use a notebook or a simple phone app to record daily feed. Subtract any feed left in the trough.

If your FCR is higher than 3.0, something is wrong. Maybe the feed is poor quality, the pigs are sick, or you are overfeeding. Check for feed wastage: holes in troughs, rodents, or birds. Also, make sure pigs have clean water. Without water, they eat less and grow slower.

Good FCR saves money. If your FCR is 2.5 instead of 3.0, you save 0.5 kg of feed per kg of gain. For a 100 kg pig, that's 50 kg of feed saved. At 20,000 Naira per 50 kg, that's 20,000 Naira saved per pig. With 20 pigs, you save 400,000 Naira. So, calculate FCR every month and aim to keep it below 2.8.

lessons.title: Target FCR of 2.5
lessons.body:
A target Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) of 2.5 is the gold standard for pig farmers. It means your pigs gain 1 kg of weight for every 2.5 kg of feed they eat. Achieving this target requires good genetics, proper nutrition, and excellent management. It is not easy, but it is possible and very profitable.

To hit FCR 2.5, start with healthy piglets from a good breed. Crossbreeds like Large White and Landrace grow faster and convert feed better than local breeds. Buy piglets from a reputable breeder. Also, feed them a balanced diet. Use a feed formula that matches their stage. For nursery pigs, feed should have 18-20% protein. For growers, 16% protein. For finishers, 14% protein. Add vitamins and minerals.

Water is critical. Pigs need clean water at all times. A lactating sow drinks up to 20 liters a day. A growing pig drinks 5-10 liters. If water is limited, feed intake drops and FCR worsens. Use nipple drinkers or clean troughs. Check water flow daily.

Health management also affects FCR. Sick pigs eat less and grow slowly. Vaccinate against common diseases like swine fever and pneumonia. Deworm regularly. Keep pens clean and dry. Avoid overcrowding. A pig needs at least 1 square meter of space in the grower stage.

Monitor FCR monthly. If it is above 2.8, find the cause. Weigh feed and pigs accurately. If you achieve 2.5, your cost per kg of pig is lower. For example, if feed is 20,000 Naira per 50 kg (400 Naira per kg), then feed cost per kg gain is 2.5 x 400 = 1,000 Naira. If FCR is 3.0, it is 1,200 Naira. That 200 Naira difference per kg adds up to 20,000 Naira for a 100 kg pig. So, aim for 2.5.

lessons.title: Buying Feed in Bulk
lessons.body:
Buying feed in bulk is one of the easiest ways to cut costs on your pig farm. When you buy in large quantities, you get discounts, save on transport, and ensure you never run out of feed. But you must store it properly to avoid spoilage.

First, calculate your total feed need for a batch. For 20 pigs from nursery to market, you need about 4,340 kg (as calculated earlier). That is roughly 87 bags of 50 kg. If you buy one bag at a time, you might pay 22,000 Naira per bag. But if you buy 50 bags or more, you can negotiate down to 20,000 Naira per bag. That saves 2,000 Naira per bag, or 174,000 Naira for the batch.

Buy from a reputable feed mill or supplier. Check the feed quality: it should smell fresh, not moldy. Look at the production date. Feed older than 3 months loses vitamins. Buy from a supplier who delivers to your farm to save transport costs. Some mills offer credit if you are a regular customer.

Storage is key. Keep feed in a dry, cool place. Use pallets to raise bags off the floor. Stack bags no more than 10 high to prevent crushing. Keep away from walls to allow air circulation. Use airtight containers for opened bags. Add a desiccant like silica gel to prevent moisture. Check for rodents and insects. Use traps or cats.

If you mix your own feed, buy ingredients in bulk: maize, soya meal, fish meal, and premix. Maize can be stored in silos or airtight bags. Buy during harvest season when prices are low. For example, maize is cheaper in November after harvest. Store it properly and use it over 3-4 months. Bulk buying requires planning but pays off.

lessons.title: Mixing Your Own Feed
lessons.body:
Mixing your own pig feed can save you 20-30% on feed costs. It gives you control over ingredients and quality. But you must get the formula right, or your pigs will grow slowly. Here is a simple guide to mixing feed for different stages.

You need a feed mixer or a clean concrete floor and a shovel. Weigh ingredients accurately using a scale. For nursery pigs (weaning to 10 weeks), mix: 50% maize, 25% soya meal, 15% fish meal, 5% milk powder, 3% vegetable oil, 1% minerals and vitamins, 1% salt. This gives about 20% protein. Mix well and feed fresh.

For grower pigs (10-16 weeks), use: 60% maize, 20% soya meal, 10% fish meal, 5% wheat bran, 3% minerals and vitamins, 1% salt, 1% limestone. This gives about 16% protein. For finisher pigs (16 weeks to market), use: 70% maize, 15% soya meal, 5% fish meal, 5% wheat bran, 3% minerals and vitamins, 1% salt, 1% limestone. This gives about 14% protein.

You can substitute some ingredients. Cassava can replace up to 30% of maize if dried and ground. Palm kernel cake can replace some soya but not more than 10%. Always add a premix that contains vitamins and minerals. Without it, pigs get sick.

Mix in small batches to ensure uniformity. Use a shovel to turn the pile at least three times. Store in clean bags. Make only enough for 2 weeks to prevent mold. If you see clumps or smell mold, throw it away. Moldy feed can kill pigs. Start by mixing for a few pigs, then scale up as you gain confidence.

lessons.title: The Cost of Bad Feed
lessons.body:
Bad feed is the most expensive mistake a pig farmer can make. It can kill your pigs, slow their growth, and waste your money. Bad feed includes moldy, expired, or nutritionally deficient feed. Understanding the cost helps you avoid it.

Moldy feed contains aflatoxins, poisons produced by mold. Aflatoxins damage the liver and immune system. Pigs may eat less, grow slowly, and die. If you feed moldy maize, you might lose 10-20% of your pigs. For 20 pigs, that's 2-4 dead pigs. At 50,000 Naira per pig, that's 100,000-200,000 Naira lost. Plus, you wasted the feed money. Always check feed for mold. If it smells musty or has green spots, do not use it.

Expired feed loses vitamins and energy. Feed older than 3 months has less nutritional value. Pigs eat more but gain less. Your FCR goes up. For example, if FCR rises from 2.5 to 3.5, you need 1 extra kg of feed per kg gain. For a 100 kg pig, that's 100 kg extra feed, costing 40,000 Naira. With 20 pigs, that's 800,000 Naira wasted. Always check production dates and use feed within 3 months.

Nutritionally deficient feed lacks protein, vitamins, or minerals. This happens when you mix your own feed without a proper formula. Pigs grow slowly and get sick. You might think you are saving money, but you are losing more. For example, if you skip the premix, pigs may get rickets or anemia. Treatment costs money and time. Always use a balanced formula and add premix.

To avoid bad feed, buy from trusted suppliers, store properly, and mix accurately. Test your feed occasionally at a lab. The cost of testing is small compared to the loss from bad feed. Remember, cheap feed is often expensive in the long run.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Feed and the Feed Budget

Feed is the single largest cost line in any pig enterprise â typically 60â75% of total production cost in African small- and medium-scale operations. For a batch farrowing system selling weaners, porkers or finished pigs daily, feed discipline is the difference between a business that pays weekly bills and one that quietly bleeds cash. This practical reference gives you the numbers, the tools and the habits that turn feed from a vague expense into a controlled, budgeted input.

The goal is simple: get pigs to market weight on the least kilograms of feed, at the lowest cost per kilogram of gain, without compromising health or growth. Everything below serves that goal.

Feed Per Stage: Nursery to Finisher

Pigs eat different amounts and different feed types at each stage of life. Knowing the expected intake per stage lets you budget accurately and spot trouble early (a pig eating too little is sick; a pig eating too much may be wasting feed or the ration may be poorly balanced).

In practice, a weaner enters the nursery at 7â10 kg and leaves at 25â30 kg; the grower stage runs from 30 to 60 kg; the finisher stage from 60 to 90â100 kg. Over the whole cycle a pig consumes roughly 230â280 kg of feed to reach 90 kg live weight, depending on genetics, health and feed quality.

Calculating Feed Conversion Ratio

Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR) is the kilogrammes of feed required to produce one kilogramme of live weight gain. It is the single most important efficiency number in your business.

FCR = Total feed consumed (kg) Ã· Total weight gain (kg)

Example: a batch of 20 pigs consumes 4,600 kg of feed and gains 2,000 kg of live weight. FCR = 4,600 Ã· 2,000 = 2.3. If the same batch had consumed 5,000 kg for the same gain, FCR = 2.5 â and every 0.1 of FCR on a 20-pig batch costs roughly one extra 50 kg bag of feed for nothing.

Target FCR of 2.5

A target FCR of 2.5 is realistic and commercially sound for smallholder and emerging commercial pig units in Africa using good-quality commercial or well-mixed home rations. Top commercial units achieve 2.2â2.4; poorly managed units sit at 3.0â3.5 or worse.

Table 1: Indicative feed use and FCR by stage (pig from 10 kg to 90 kg)
Stage Weight range (kg) Days Feed per pig (kg) Target FCR
Nursery10â3035351.75
Grower30â6045903.00
Finisher60â90451353.00
Whole cycle10â901252602.5â3.0

Source: Adapted from FAO Pig Sector Development Guidelines and NRC Nutrient Requirements of Swine (2012). Actual values vary with genetics, health, climate and feed quality.

Buying Feed in Bulk

Bulk buying is the fastest way to cut your feed cost per kilogram. In most African markets, a 50 kg bag bought singly costs 10â25% more than the same feed bought in 20-bag (1 tonne) lots. If you batch-farrow, you already have predictable volumes â use that predictability to negotiate.

  • Group with neighbours. Form a buying group of 3â5 farmers and order by the tonne to unlock wholesale prices.
  • Buy raw materials, not just finished feed. Maize, soya, sunflower cake and fishmeal bought at harvest are far cheaper than finished pellets.
  • Store properly. Airtight drums, pallets off the floor, dry ventilated store. Weevils, rats and mould destroy 5â10% of stored feed in poor conditions.
  • Never buy more than 4â6 weeks of feed unless storage is excellent â vitamin potency and fat quality decline.

Mixing Your Own Feed

On-farm mixing can cut feed cost by 20â35% versus commercial pellets, provided you get the ration right and the ingredients are consistent. A simple, practical grower ration for African conditions:

Table 2: Simple home-mixed grower ration (per 100 kg)
IngredientQuantity (kg)Role
Maize (ground)60Energy
Soya bean meal20Protein
Sunflower or cotton cake10Protein / cost filler
Wheat bran7Fibre / bulk
Fishmeal (or blood meal)2Animal protein
Mineralâvitamin premix0.7Micronutrients
Salt (NaCl)0.3Electrolytes
Total100~16% crude protein

Source: Adapted from FAO Good Practices for Animal Feed and Feeding and ILRI smallholder pig feeding guides. Always confirm premix inclusion rate with the supplier.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Aflatoxin and Mould

Never feed maize, groundnut cake or any grain that is mouldy, musty-smelling, discoloured or clumped. Aflatoxin from Aspergillus flavus causes liver damage, poor growth, suppressed immunity and residues in pork â and it is not destroyed by cooking or pelleting at normal temperatures. In humid African conditions, buy only dry grain (below 13% moisture), store on pallets in a dry, ventilated room, and use within 4 weeks. If in doubt, throw it out â the cost of one bad batch is far less than the cost of a dead or stunted batch of pigs. Source: FAO/WHO Codex Alimentarius and IITA aflatoxin control guidelines.

The Cost of Bad Feed

Bad feed is not just feed that is spoiled. It is also feed that is wrong for the stage, poorly balanced, or inconsistent. The hidden costs are brutal:

  • Higher FCR. A ration 10% short on protein can push FCR from 2.5 to 3.2 â that is 70 extra kg of feed per pig.
  • Slower growth. Pigs take 20â30 extra days to reach market, tying up pens and delaying your next batch.
  • Disease and mortality. Mycotoxins and nutrient deficiencies open the door to diarrhoea, respiratory disease and sudden death.
  • Poor carcass quality. Buyers discount soft, pale or low-yielding carcasses.

On a 20-pig batch, an FCR blowout from 2.5 to 3.0 can wipe out your entire margin. Feed quality is not a place to save money â it is a place to invest money wisely.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Weigh feed, don't guess. Use a hanging scale or calibrated scoop for every feed. Eyeballing overfeeds by 10â15%.
  2. Track FCR every batch. Record total feed in and total live weight out. Review against the 2.5 target.
  3. Match feed to stage. Nursery, grower and finisher rations are not interchangeable.
  4. Buy in bulk or group-buy. Aim for tonne-level purchases to cut unit cost 10â25%.
  5. Store dry, cool and off the floor. Use pallets, airtight containers, and first-in-first-out stock rotation.
  6. Test raw materials for moisture and mould before mixing. Reject anything above 13% moisture.
  7. Mix accurately. Weigh premix and minerals â never approximate. Poor mixing causes uneven growth.
  8. Watch water. Pigs drink 2â3 litres per kg of feed. Clean, cool water is part of the feed budget.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Good Practices for Animal Feed and Feeding
  • FAO â Pig Sector Development Guidelines
  • ILRI â Smallholder Pig Production Resources
  • IITA â Aflatoxin Control in Africa
  • NRC â Nutrient Requirements of Swine (11th revised edition)

Practical Reference â Module: Feed and the Feed Budget. Course: Daily Pig Sales: Batch Farrowing System. Rise AFRICA Skills.

quiz.q: How much feed does a nursery pig eat per day?
quiz.explanation: Nursery piglets eat about 0.5 kg per day.

quiz.q: What is the total feed needed for one pig from nursery to market?
quiz.explanation: 14 kg nursery + 63 kg grower + 140 kg finisher = 217 kg.

quiz.q: Which stage requires feed with the highest protein content?
quiz.explanation: Nursery feed needs 18-20% protein, the highest of all stages.

quiz.q: How do you calculate Feed Conversion Ratio (FCR)?
options: A) Total weight gained Ã· total feed eaten
B) Total feed eaten Ã· total weight gained
C) Total feed eaten Ã total weight gained
D) Total weight gained - total feed eaten
quiz.explanation: FCR = total feed eaten divided by total weight gained.

quiz.q: If 10 pigs eat 1,000 kg of feed and gain 400 kg, what is the FCR?
What does an FCR of 2.5 mean?
options: A) 2.5 kg of feed produces 1 kg of pig
B) 1 kg of feed produces 2.5 kg of pig
C) 2.5 pigs eat 1 kg of feed
D) 1 pig eats 2.5 kg of feed daily
quiz.explanation: FCR 2.5 means 2.5 kg feed per 1 kg weight gain.

quiz.q: What is a sign that your FCR might be too high?
options: A) Pigs are gaining weight quickly
C) Pigs have plenty of water
D) You are using a feed scale
quiz.explanation: Feed waste increases FCR.

quiz.q: Why is water important for good FCR?
options: B) Pigs drink more and eat more
quiz.explanation: Without water, pigs eat less and grow slower, worsening FCR.

quiz.q: What is the target FCR for profitable pig farming?
quiz.explanation: A target FCR of 2.5 is considered ideal.

quiz.q: Which breed is known for better feed conversion?
quiz.explanation: Crossbreeds like Large White and Landrace grow faster and convert feed better.

quiz.q: How much water does a lactating sow drink per day?
quiz.explanation: A lactating sow can drink up to 20 liters daily.

quiz.q: What is the minimum space needed per pig in the grower stage?
quiz.explanation: Each grower pig needs at least 1 square meter of space.

quiz.q: If feed costs 400 Naira per kg and FCR is 2.5, what is the feed cost per kg gain?
How many bags of 50 kg feed are needed for 20 pigs from nursery to market?
quiz.explanation: 4,340 kg Ã· 50 kg = 86.8, about 87 bags.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of buying feed in bulk?
options: C) More frequent trips to market
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying usually gives discounts and saves on transport.

quiz.q: How should feed bags be stored?
options: B) On pallets off the floor
quiz.explanation: Pallets keep feed off the floor and prevent moisture damage.

quiz.q: When is maize usually cheapest to buy in bulk?
quiz.explanation: Maize prices are lowest right after harvest.

quiz.q: What is the protein content of a good grower feed?
quiz.explanation: Grower feed should have about 16% protein.

quiz.q: Which ingredient can replace up to 30% of maize in pig feed?
quiz.explanation: Dried and ground cassava can replace up to 30% of maize.

quiz.q: Why is premix important in homemade feed?
options: B) It provides vitamins and minerals
quiz.explanation: Premix supplies essential vitamins and minerals to prevent deficiency diseases.

quiz.q: How often should you mix feed to avoid mold?
quiz.explanation: Mix only enough for 2 weeks to prevent mold growth.

quiz.q: What is aflatoxin?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is a toxic substance produced by mold.

quiz.q: What can happen if you feed moldy feed to pigs?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxins damage the liver and can cause death.

quiz.q: How much can you lose if FCR rises from 2.5 to 3.5 for a 100 kg pig?
quiz.explanation: FCR increase of 1.0 means 1 extra kg feed per kg gain, so 100 kg extra for 100 kg pig.

quiz.q: What is a sign of nutritionally deficient feed?
options: A) Pigs grow slowly and get sick
quiz.explanation: Deficient feed lacks nutrients, causing slow growth and illness.

quiz.q: Why is it important to check feed production date?
options: A) To know when to plant maize
B) To ensure feed is not expired
quiz.explanation: Expired feed loses nutritional value and can harm pigs.

quiz.q: What is the best way to store opened feed bags?
quiz.explanation: Airtight containers prevent moisture and pests.

quiz.q: What is the cost of bad feed in terms of pig deaths?
quiz.explanation: Moldy feed can cause 10-20% mortality.

quiz.q: How can you test feed quality?
quiz.explanation: Both sensory checks and lab tests help ensure feed quality.

quiz.q: What is the first step to mixing your own feed?
quiz.explanation: Accurate weighing is crucial for a balanced feed formula.
